summary: This informational RFC gives an overview of IETF network management standards, summarizing existing and ongoing work on standards-track management protocols and data models. It points to other overview documents and classifies the standards to help developers and users choose appropriate ones.

eli5.summary: This is a map of the tools for looking after computer networks. It says which tool is for what job.

subtitle: A comprehensive guide to IETF network management protocols and data models.

tldr.problem: Network operators need a variety of management protocols and data models to monitor and configure network devices, but the IETF has standardized many competing approaches with different strengths and purposes.
tldr.mechanism: This informational RFC catalogs the major IETF management protocols (SNMP, Syslog, IPFIX, NETCONF) and specialized protocols (DHCP, RADIUS, Diameter), organizes them by use case, and provides data models for common management tasks.
tldr.outcome: Operators and protocol designers can use this overview to understand the management protocol landscape, select appropriate tools for their needs, and identify any gaps in standardization.
tldr.outcomeLabel: A map of the management toolbox

today: RFC 6632 is an Informational RFC that provides a comprehensive overview of IETF network management standards as of 2012. It remains a reference for understanding the management protocol landscape, though the IETF has continued to extend YANG data models and NETCONF capabilities since publication. It is not superseded.

sections.title: Understanding Network Management
sections.content:
Network management consists of monitoring devices and networks for faults, configuring devices and services, tracking usage and billing (accounting), analyzing performance, and securing the network. The IETF has standardized numerous protocols and data models for these tasks, but the landscape is complex.

This RFC serves as a comprehensive overview of the IETF Standards Track management protocols and data models, intended for protocol designers choosing management approaches, operators selecting tools, and standards development organizations planning to use IETF management technologies. It classifies standards to help readers navigate the landscape, from the core pull-based monitoring system SNMP to the push-based configuration protocol NETCONF, to specialized protocols for address management, policy, and authentication.
sections.eli5: Networks need many different tools to stay healthy. This RFC explains what tools the IETF has made and what each one does.

sections.title: Core Management Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC identifies four foundational management protocols. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is the most widely deployed, using a pull model where a manager station interrogates agents on network devices using a standardized set of managed objects called MIBs. SNMPv3 adds security with user-based authentication and privacy. SNMP works well for fault and performance monitoring and is used with counters to track packet and byte flows.

Syslog is a complementary push-based logging mechanism where devices send timestamped event messages to a central collector. It is simple and lightweight, with optional TLS encryption. IPFIX (IP Flow Information Export) is a push-based protocol that exports flow records for usage-based accounting and traffic analysis, using a template-based format for efficiency. NETCONF (Network Configuration Protocol) is a transaction-oriented configuration management protocol using an XML-based encoding over SSH or TLS, providing atomic commits and rollback capabilities. YANG is the data modeling language for NETCONF, offering hierarchical data definitions with clear distinctions between configuration and operational state.
sections.eli5: SNMP asks devices questions and collects answers. Syslog listens for devices to report problems. IPFIX counts the traffic flowing between machines. NETCONF changes configurations safely. YANG is the language for describing what can be configured.

sections.title: Specialized Management and Control Protocols
sections.content:
Beyond the core protocols, the IETF has standardized specialized protocols for specific management domains. DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) assigns IP addresses and configuration parameters to devices. RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) provides centralized authentication, authorization, and accounting (AAA) for network access. Diameter is a more flexible successor to RADIUS with improved error handling and support for roaming.

Other specialized protocols address particular network management needs: IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) defines how to measure network performance in a standardized way; SNMP notifications (Traps) provide asynchronous event delivery; Policy-Based Management (COPS and policy frameworks) allow operators to define rules for network behavior; Syslog extensions support structured data and signed messages for audit trails. For specific domains, the IETF has also standardized CAPWAP for wireless access point control, ANCP for broadband access node control, and ACAP for application configuration.
sections.eli5: Some protocols handle special jobs: DHCP hands out IP addresses, RADIUS checks passwords, Diameter does both at scale. IPPM measures how fast the network is. Policies let operators make rules instead of configuring each device by hand.

sections.title: Network Management Data Models
sections.content:
The protocols carry management data that must be consistently structured across different vendors and devices. Management Information Bases (MIBs) defined in SMIv2 (Structure of Management Information Version 2) provide the standard object definitions for SNMP. The RFC catalogs MIBs for infrastructure (entity information, interfaces), link-layer concerns, network-layer protocols (IP, routing), transport-layer issues, and application-layer monitoring.

The RFC also organizes data models using the FCAPS framework (Fault, Configuration, Accounting, Performance, Security management), mapping standards to these five management domains. New work has shifted toward YANG data models used with NETCONF for more flexible configuration management. The RFC also references IPFIX Information Elements for flow-based accounting, Syslog Structured Data Elements for logging, and identifies gaps in areas like sensor network management and OAM (Operations, Administration, and Maintenance) for specific technologies.
sections.eli5: All management tools need a common language for describing what they manage. MIBs are the old way (for SNMP). YANG is the new way (for NETCONF). Both let vendors describe their equipment consistently.

sections.title: Related Standards and Future Work
sections.content:
The RFC references related IETF work on management: RFC 3535 documented strengths and weaknesses of IETF management protocols from a 2002 IAB workshop; RFC 5706 recommends that protocol designers consider management needs early; RFC 4221 describes MPLS management architecture; RFC 6371 covers OAM frameworks for MPLS-based transport networks.

The RFC also identifies emerging management challenges. At the time of publication, energy management (EMAN working group) was a new focus area. Sensor networks and constrained devices were not yet addressed with specific IETF technologies, relying instead on simple application-layer protocols. The RFC does not cover OAM for the data plane (such as MPLS-TP OAM), noting that these are covered separately. This comprehensive overview serves as both a reference for what exists and a guide to where gaps remain.
sections.eli5: The RFC also looks back at lessons learned and forward at new challenges like managing power consumption and tiny devices.
